title: Relational Spacetime: A Systemic Conceptual Framework for Couples Therapy
abstract: ABSTRACT Contemporary couple relationships are negotiated within increasingly complex temporal and spatial conditions shaped by different contexts like work, caring responsibilities, social acceleration and digital connectivity. This paper proposes relational spacetime as a clinical and conceptual framework for examining how time and space become mutually organised within couple relationships. Drawing on systemic therapy, distinctions between clock‐time and lived time, temporal desynchronisation, attachment theory, structural perspectives on relational space and sociological accounts of social acceleration, the framework examines how partners may inhabit different temporal and spatial worlds while negotiating their positions. Relational spacetime is presented as a sensitising framework rather than as a new theory of time and space in therapy, bringing together temporal and spatial dimensions of recursive couple patterns. It extends the Milan‐influenced tradition of attention to lived time, and its distinctive contribution lies in holding temporal and spatial organisation together within a single relational field. The paper also considers the therapist's use of questions, interruptions, silence, rhythm and advanced strategic tasks as interventions in relational time and space. Particular attention is given to the relationship between second‐order systemic reflexivity and advanced strategic therapy. Drawing on Cecchin's curiosity and irreverence, on second‐order cybernetics (Von Foerster, 2003), and, critically, on Smith's (2023) concept of 1.5‐order therapy, the paper argues that strategic directiveness need not imply first‐order epistemological certainty, that it can be practised from a fully second‐order position without appeal to an intermediate order and that therapeutic strategy can involve intentional and directive action while remaining tentative, provisional, reflexive and open to the revision of the hypotheses through the couple's response. Relational spacetime is therefore offered as a question‐generating framework for exploring how temporal and spatial patterns, social arrangements and therapeutic interventions shape the possibilities for connection, distance and change.
